Random pair split over only 60 proteins suggests leakage. Let me check.I've drafted the Results paragraph, but I left out the generalization claim because the data doesn't support it.

**Why the claim fails.** Every test pair uses proteins that also appear in training (140 of 140, with all 60 proteins in train). A baseline that ignores sequence completely does as well as PairNet. It scores a test pair by summing each protein's interaction rate in the training set. Its test AUROC is 0.795, against PairNet's 0.79. So the 0.79 can be explained by PairNet learning which proteins tend to interact, without learning anything about pair-specific sequence determinants.

**Draft Results paragraph:**

> On the 140 held-out protein pairs (22.9% positive), PairNet achieved an AUROC of 0.79 (95% bootstrap CI 0.70–0.88). However, the split was random at the pair level, so every test protein also appeared in the training set (60 proteins in total). A sequence-free baseline that scores each pair by the training-set interaction rates of its two proteins achieved a comparable AUROC of 0.79 (0.795). PairNet's performance is therefore consistent with learning protein-level propensities to interact (for example, hub-like or non-interacting proteins) and provides no evidence that it captures pair-specific sequence determinants or generalizes to unseen proteins. Evaluating this would require a split in which test pairs contain proteins held out from training, ideally with neither protein seen, and ideally with sequence-similarity-aware clustering.

**Caveats.**
- The CI comes from 140 pairs, so it is wide.
- I didn't have PairNet's training code or embeddings, so I could only evaluate the saved predictions.
- Before you state the claim or use PairNet to predict partners for uncharacterized proteins, re-run it with a protein-disjoint split. That setting matches the intended use.
